title: Warm Climates May Have Helped Crocodile Kin Outlast the Dinosaurs
paragraphs: The asteroid that closed the Cretaceous some 66 million years ago extinguished the non-avian dinosaurs, yet the crocodile's lineage trundled on regardless. A study led by University College London and published in Science Advances proposes that an old and abiding fondness for warmth may have been the animals' saving grace.

The team marshalled more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species, inferred the temperatures and rainfall each tolerated, and tested those preferences against climate and geography simulations reaching back 245 million years. When the post-impact world was modelled with sunlight dimmed by 5% or 10% by dust and ash, warm equatorial belts remained hospitable to crocodile relatives, whereas a 15% dimming left almost nowhere habitable, a scenario the authors deem unlikely. By the same group's earlier reckoning, the ground available to non-avian dinosaurs shrank considerably more.

None of this amounts to proof. The refuges are inferred from models rather than observed in the rock record, and the authors take pains to say that warmth was probably but one thread in a tapestry that also included modest size, a half-aquatic existence, adaptable appetites and thrifty metabolisms. They also warn that roads, farms and cities may now block crocodiles from tracking suitable climates as the world heats up. Funding came from the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust and the Natural Environment Research Council.

questions.q: What does 'saving grace' mean in the first paragraph?
questions.a: A quality that rescued the animals from a bad situation.
By inference from climate models, not direct observation.

questions.q: What does the idiom 'one thread in a tapestry' imply?
questions.a: Warmth was only one of several contributing factors.
